claim: Basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors encoded by RSL class I genes control a gene regulatory network that positively regulates the development of filamentous rooting cells – root hairs and rhizoids – in land plants.
source: Basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors encoded by RSL class I genes control a gene regulatory network that positively regulates the development of filamentous rooting cells – root hairs and rhizoids – in land plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: The GLABRA2 transcription factor negatively regulates RSL class I genes in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: The GLABRA2 transcription factor negatively regulates these genes in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on GLABRA2 function.

claim: A mutant screen in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha identified FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1) microRNA (miRNA) that negatively regulates the RSL class I gene MpRSL1.
source: To find negative regulators of RSL class I genes in early diverging land plants we conducted a mutant screen in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha. This identified FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1) microRNA (miRNA) that negatively regulates the RSL class I gene MpRSL1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutant screen described in the manuscript.

claim: The MpFRH1 miRNA and its mRNA target constitute a feedback mechanism that controls epidermal cell differentiation.
source: The miRNA and its mRNA target constitute a feedback mechanism that controls epidermal cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mutual regulation between MpFRH1 and MpRSL1.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA target sites are conserved among liverwort RSL class I mRNAs but are not present in RSL class I mRNAs of other land plants.
source: MpFRH1 miRNA target sites are conserved among liverwort RSL class I mRNAs but are not present in RSL class I mRNAs of other land plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript.

claim: While RSL class I genes are ancient and conserved, independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution.
source: These findings indicate that while RSL class I genes are ancient and conserved, independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparative data showing different negative regulators in different lineages.

claim: The rooting structures of the first land plants are likely to have comprised systems of tip-growing filamentous cells called rhizoids that are morphologically similar to root hairs of vascular plants.
source: The rooting structures of the first land plants are likely to have comprised systems of tip-growing filamentous cells called rhizoids that are morphologically similar to root hairs of vascular plants (Edwards et al., 1995; Wellman et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2005; Kerp et al., 2003; Taylor, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior paleobotanical research.

claim: RSL class I genes promote root hair differentiation in the vascular plants rice (Oryza sativa), Brachypodium distachyon and Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: RSL class I genes promote root hair differentiation in the vascular plants rice (Oryza sativa), Brachypodium distachyon and Arabidopsis thaliana (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Menand et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I genes in these species.

claim: RSL class I genes positively regulate rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and rhizoid development in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha and the moss Physcomitrella patens.
source: Similarly, RSL class I genes positively regulate rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and rhizoid development in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha and the moss Physcomitrella patens (Proust et al., 2016; Menand et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I genes in bryophytes.

claim: Root hairs and rhizoids initiate from those epidermal cells that express RSL class I genes.
source: Root hairs and rhizoids initiate from those epidermal cells that express RSL class I genes (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Menand et al., 2007; Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I gene expression patterns.

claim: Constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes is sufficient to modulate root hair patterning by inducing root hair development from any root epidermal cell in the monocots O. sativa and B. distachyon.
source: Furthermore, constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes is sufficient to modulate root hair patterning by inducing root hair development from any root epidermal cell in the monocots O. sativa and B. distachyon (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I gene overexpression.

claim: Constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes in the liverwort M. polymorpha and moss P. patens is sufficient to induce rhizoid formation from almost any epidermal cell of the gametophyte.
source: Similarly, constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes in the liverwort M. polymorpha and moss P. patens is sufficient to induce rhizoid formation from almost any epidermal cell of the gametophyte (Proust et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I gene overexpression in bryophytes.

claim: RSL class I genes function as molecular switches that are both necessary and sufficient to induce the root hair cell and rhizoid cell developmental program in epidermal cells.
source: These findings indicate that RSL class I genes function as molecular switches that are both necessary and sufficient to induce the root hair cell and rhizoid cell developmental program in epidermal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited overexpression and loss-of-function studies.

claim: The RSL class I mechanism is likely to be ancient and have originated in the common ancestor of all land plants.
source: This suggests that the RSL class I mechanism is likely to be ancient and have originated in the common ancestor of all land plants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the conservation of RSL class I gene function across land plant lineages.

claim: RSL class I genes from the moss P. patens, liverwort M. polymorpha or monocot rice restore root hair development in the roothairless A. thaliana mutants that lack RSL class I gene function.
source: RSL class I genes from the moss P. patens, liverwort M. polymorpha or monocot rice restore root hair development in the roothairless A. thaliana mutants that lack RSL class I gene function (Menand et al., 2007; Proust et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on cross-species complementation experiments.

claim: The molecular function of RSL class I proteins is conserved among moss, liverwort, rice, and Arabidopsis lineages.
source: This indicates that the molecular function of RSL class I proteins is conserved among these lineages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the complementation data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Negative regulation of RSL class I genes in A. thaliana suppresses the formation of root hairs in a subset of root epidermal cells.
source: Negative regulation of RSL class I genes in A. thaliana suppresses the formation of root hairs in a subset of root epidermal cells (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on negative regulation in Arabidopsis.

claim: The A. thaliana root epidermis comprises two cell types; trichoblasts that go on to differentiate into root hair cells and atrichoblasts that differentiate as root hairless epidermal cells.
source: The A. thaliana root epidermis comprises two cell types; trichoblasts that go on to differentiate into root hair cells and atrichoblasts that differentiate as root hairless epidermal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Arabidopsis root epidermis development.

claim: RSL class I genes, AtRHD6 and AtRSL1, are expressed early in development of trichoblasts before root hairs emerge and they positively regulate the expression of genes involved in root hair differentiation.
source: RSL class I genes, AtRHD6 and AtRSL1, are expressed early in development of trichoblasts before root hairs emerge and they positively regulate the expression of genes involved in root hair differentiation (Menand et al., 2007; Yi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression and function.

claim: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression is repressed in atrichoblasts by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2).
source: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression is repressed in atrichoblasts by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2) (Di Cristina et al., 1996; Bernhardt et al., 2005; Bernhardt et al., 2003; Koshino-Kimura et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on GL2 function.

claim: AtGL2 proteins directly bind to L1 box motifs on the promoters of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 and inhibit root hair initiation by repressing the transcription of these positive regulators of root hair development.
source: AtGL2 proteins directly bind to L1 box motifs on the promoters of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 and inhibit root hair initiation by repressing the transcription of these positive regulators of root hair development (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on GL2 binding and function.

claim: GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes (liverworts, mosses and hornworts).
source: Furthermore, GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes (liverworts, mosses and hornworts) (Zalewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on GL2 gene distribution.

claim: Four mutants, ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10, develop no or very few rhizoid precursor cells and consequently develop few rhizoids.
source: We identified four mutants, ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 that develop no or very few rhizoid precursor cells and consequently develop few rhizoids (Figure 1A–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and microscopy images shown in Figure 1.

claim: The few rhizoids phenotype segregated as a single locus in the F1 generation of ST45-2 and ST49-10 backcrosses to wild type.
source: The few rhizoids phenotype segregated as a single locus in each F1 generation, that is 50% of plants developed few rhizoids and 50% were indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by segregation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The few rhizoids phenotype co-segregated with the hygromycin resistance marker gene on the T-DNA in both ST45-2 and ST49-10 segregating F1 populations.
source: Furthermore, the few rhizoids phenotype co-segregated with the hygromycin resistance marker gene on the T-DNA in both ST45-2 and ST49-10 segregating F1 populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-segregation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a single T-DNA insertion that is tightly linked to the few rhizoids phenotype in ST45-2.
source: Based on the ratios of hygromycin resistant to hygromycin sensitive F1 plants, there is a single T-DNA insertion that is tightly linked to the few rhizoids phenotype in ST45-2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the segregation ratios observed in the F1 generation.

claim: There are two T-DNA insertions in ST49-10; one responsible for the few rhizoids phenotype and a second unlinked T-DNA insertion.
source: There are two T-DNA insertions in ST49-10; one responsible for the few rhizoids phenotype and a second unlinked T-DNA insertion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the segregation ratios observed in the F1 generation.

claim: A T-DNA insertion was identified within a 1.2 kb region of the M. polymorpha genome in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10.
source: We identified a T-DNA insertion within a 1.2 kb region of the M. polymorpha genome in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 (Figure 1M, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that this genomic region is involved in rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by TAIL-PCR data and the T-DNA insertion map shown in Figure 1M.

claim: No transcript overlapped with the T-DNA insertion sites in any of the four few rhizoids mutants based on mapping the M. polymorpha gametophyte transcriptome sequences onto the genome assembly.
source: Mapping the M. polymorpha gametophyte transcriptome sequences onto the genome assembly (Honkanen et al., 2016) indicated that no transcript overlapped with the T-DNA insertion sites in any of the four few rhizoids mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: A transcript fragment that mapped next to the right border of the T-DNA insertions was expressed at higher levels in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 than in wild type.
source: A transcript fragment that mapped next to the right border of the T-DNA insertions was expressed at higher levels in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 than in wild type (Figure 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: 3' and 5' RACE-PCR identified a 1.2 kb intron-less polyadenylated transcript named FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1).
source: To identify the full-length transcript we performed 3' and 5' RACE-PCR. This identified a 1.2 kb intron-less polyadenylated transcript (Supplementary file 2) that we named FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE-PCR experimental data.

claim: In each of the four few rhizoids mutants a T-DNA is inserted 5' of a gene encoding a 1.2 kb transcript that is expressed at higher levels than in wild type.
source: Together these data indicate that in each of the four few rhizoids mutants a T-DNA is inserted 5' of a gene encoding a 1.2 kb transcript that is expressed at higher levels than in wild type.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the T-DNA insertion mapping and expression data.

claim: The majority of plants transformed with MpFRH1 under the control of the strong constitutive rice ACTIN1 promoter (88 out of 103) developed very few or no rhizoids.
source: The majority of the resulting transformed plants (88 out of 103) developed very few or no rhizoids (Figure 2C,G,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments and images in Figure 2.

claim: Steady state levels of MpFRH1 transcript were higher than wild type in each of the transformed lines with few rhizoids, while wild type levels of MpFRH1 transcript were observed in the lines with wild type phenotype.
source: Steady state levels of MpFRH1 transcript were higher than wild type in each of the transformed lines with few rhizoids, while wild type levels of MpFRH1 transcript were observed in the lines with wild type phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over-expression of the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype of the ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 T-DNA insertion mutants.
source: This indicates that over-expression of the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype of the ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 T-DNA insertion mutants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overexpression and phenotype data.

claim: Each of ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 is a gain-of-function mutant, in which elevated expression of MpFRH1 results in reduced number of rhizoid precursor cells and rhizoids.
source: This suggests that each is a gain-of-function mutant, in which elevated expression of MpFRH1 results in reduced number of rhizoid precursor cells and rhizoids.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overexpression and mutant phenotype data.

claim: MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
source: Together these findings indicate that MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the gain-of-function mutant and overexpression data.

claim: MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines lacked multicellular mucilage papillae that develop in the epidermis near meristematic regions of wild type plants.
source: Furthermore, like Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants, MpFRH1GOF mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines lacked multicellular mucilage papillae that develop in the epidermis near meristematic regions of wild type plants (Figure 2Q–T).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2Q-T.

claim: Gemmae only rarely develop in Mprsl1, MpFRH1GOF, proACT:MpFRH1 lines and the gemma cups were generally empty.
source: By contrast, gemmae only rarely develop in Mprsl1, MpFRH1GOF, proACT:MpFRH1 lines and the gemma cups were generally empty (Figure 2N–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2N-P.

claim: MpFRH1 negatively regulates the development of the same structures – rhizoids, gemmae and epidermal papillae – that are positively regulated by MpRSL1.
source: Together, these data suggest that MpFRH1 negatively regulates the development of the same structures – rhizoids, gemmae and epidermal papillae – that are positively regulated by MpRSL1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phenotypic similarities between MpFRH1 gain-of-function and Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants.

claim: There are no long open reading frames in the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript sequence and the sequence is not similar to any Arabidopsis protein coding sequences.
source: There are no long open reading frames in the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript sequence and the sequence is not similar to any Arabidopsis protein coding sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic sequence analysis.

claim: The 21 nt predicted miRNA mpo-MIR11861 (UGUGUGAGAAGAGGCCAAUGU) maps to the same genomic location as the MpFRH1 transcript.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the 21 nt predicted miRNA mpo-MIR11861 (UGUGUGAGAAGAGGCCAAUGU) maps to the same genomic location as the MpFRH1 transcript (Tsuzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior miRNA prediction work and genomic mapping.

claim: Over-expression of a 150 bp fragment of the MpFRH1 transcript containing the predicted miRNA hairpin structure in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype.
source: Over-expression of the 150 bp miRNA hairpin-containing fragment (MpFRH1miRNA) in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype (Figure 4C,I,O, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that MpFRH1 is a miRNA gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of the mature MpFRH1 miRNA was verified using stem-loop PCR.
source: The presence of the mature MpFRH1 miRNA was verified using stem-loop PCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by stem-loop PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated levels of the MpFRH1 pri-miRNA transcript in MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants give rise to elevated levels of mature MpFRH1 miRNA.
source: In the stem-loop PCR a 60 bp band corresponding to the MpFRH1 miRNA and a fused stem-loop sequence was stronger in the MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutant samples compared to wild type, suggesting that elevated levels of the MpFRH1 pri-miRNA transcript in these mutants give rise to elevated levels of mature MpFRH1 miRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from stem-loop PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transformed plants over-expressing proACT:MpFRH1noATG (with mutated start codons) developed very few rhizoids similar to the four MpFRH1GOF lines and proACT:MpFRH1 lines.
source: Transformed plants over-expressing proACT:MpFRH1noATG developed very few rhizoids similar to the four MpFRH1GOF lines and proACT:MpFRH1 lines (Figure 4D,J,P, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transformed plants overexpressing either MpFRH1PSORF1 or MpFRH1PSORF2 did not have defects in rhizoid development and were undistinguishable from wild type plants.
source: Transformed plants overexpressing either MpFRH1PSORF1 or MpFRH1PSORF2 did not have defects in rhizoid development and were undistinguishable from wild type plants (Figure 4E–F,K–L,Q–R, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA that represses rhizoid development.
source: Together, these findings indicate that MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA that represses rhizoid development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overexpression experiments with different MpFRH1 constructs.

claim: One of the predicted MpFRH1 miRNA targets was a 21 bp sequence on the MpRSL1 mRNA.
source: One of the predicted targets was a 21 bp sequence on the MpRSL1 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic target prediction using TargetFinder.

claim: The steady state levels of MpRSL1 mRNA were lower in all four MpFRH1GOF mutants and the four proACT1:MpFRH1 lines tested.
source: The steady state levels of MpRSL1 mRNA were lower in all four MpFRH1GOF mutants and the four proACT1:MpFRH1 lines tested (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The amplified MpRSL1 mRNA fragment from 5'RLM-RACE PCR assay terminated within the predicted MpFRH1 target site, indicating MpFRH1 miRNA mediates cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
source: The amplified MpRSL1 mRNA fragment terminated within the predicted MpFRH1 target site (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 3), indicating MpFRH1 miRNA mediates cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by 5'RLM-RACE PCR data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The steady state levels of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs were similar in wild type and MpFRH1 gain of function mutants suggesting that they are not MpFRH1 miRNA targets.
source: The steady state levels of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs were similar in wild type and MpFRH1 gain of function mutants suggesting that they are not MpFRH1 miRNA targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The predicted MpFRH1 miRNA target site on the orthologs of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs is not conserved among liverworts.
source: Furthermore, the predicted MpFRH1 miRNA target site on the orthologs of each of these three mRNAs is not conserved among liverworts (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates rhizoid development by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
source: We conclude that MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates rhizoid development by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RLM-RACE and expression data.

claim: Twenty-five out of the 26 transformants of MpFRH1GOF2 mutants transformed with the wild type version of MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt) were rhizoidless like MpFRH1GOF2 plants, while only one transformant developed rhizoids.
source: Twenty-five out of the 26 transformants were rhizoidless like MpFRH1GOF2 plants, while only one transformant developed rhizoids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of the wild type version of MpRSL1 from the MpEF1∝ promoter does not suppress the rhizoidless phenotype of MpFRH1GOF2.
source: This indicates that expression of the wild type version of MpRSL1 from the MpEF1∝ promoter does not suppress the rhizoidless phenotype of MpFRH1GOF2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the transformation data.

claim: Seven out of ten lines transformed with the MpFRH1 miRNA resistant version of MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res) developed abundant rhizoids on the ventral thallus surface and two lines developed rhizoids on both ventral and dorsal surfaces of the thallus, while a single line was rhizoidless.
source: Seven of these transformed lines developed abundant rhizoids on the ventral thallus surface and two lines developed rhizoids on both ventral and dorsal surfaces of the thallus, while a single line was rhizoidless and was phenotypically identical to MpFRH1GOF2 plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: None (0%) of the gemmalings expressing the wild type MpRSL1 in the MpFRH1GOF2 background (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids.
source: None (0%) of the gemmalings expressing the wild type MpRSL1 in the MpFRH1GOF2 background (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most (88.9%) gemmalings transformed with the miRNA resistant form of the MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids.
source: In contrast, most (88.9%) gemmalings transformed with the miRNA resistant form of the MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Gemmae developed in the gemma cups of MpFRH1GOF2 plants transformed with proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res, while similar to the MpFRH1GOF2 plants the gemma cups of proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2 plants were mostly empty.
source: Gemmae developed in the gemma cups of MpFRH1GOF2 plants transformed with proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res, while similar to the MpFRH1GOF2 plants the gemma cups of proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2 plants were mostly empty (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The restoration of gemma development by the proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res construct in the MpFRH1GOF2 background demonstrates that MpRSL1 is a target of MpFRH1 regulation during gemma development.
source: The restoration of gemma development by the proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res construct in the MpFRH1GOF2 background demonstrates that MpRSL1 is a target of MpFRH1 regulation during gemma development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment data.

claim: MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1 by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA during the development of structures derived from single epidermal cells in M. polymorpha.
source: Together these data are consistent with the hypothesis that MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1 by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA during the development of structures derived from single epidermal cells in M. polymorpha.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment and other data.

claim: Steady state MpFRH1 transcript levels were lower than wild type in the Mprsl1-1 and Mprsl1-2 loss-of-function mutant alleles, but higher than wild type in the MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutant alleles MpRSLGOF1-3.
source: Steady state MpFRH1 transcript levels were lower than wild type in the Mprsl1-1 and Mprsl1-2 loss-of-function mutant alleles, but higher than wild type in the MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutant alleles MpRSLGOF1-3 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: MpRSL1 positively regulates steady state MpFRH1 transcript level.
source: These results indicate that MpRSL1 positively regulates steady state MpFRH1 transcript level.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the expression data in MpRSL1 mutants.

claim: Functional MpRSL1 is not required for baseline MpFRH1 expression; a low level of MpFRH1 mRNA persists in the Mprsl1 complete loss-of-function mutant background.
source: However, functional MpRSL1 is not required for baseline MpFRH1 expression; a low level of MpFRH1 mRNA persists in the Mprsl1 complete loss-of-function mutant background (Figure 6), suggesting that other mechanisms also contribute to the regulation of MpFRH1 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The positive regulation of MpFRH1 expression by MpRSL1, which is in turn targeted by MpFRH1 miRNA, indicates that MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 miRNA form a regulatory loop with negative feedback.
source: The positive regulation of MpFRH1 expression by MpRSL1, which is in turn targeted by MpFRH1 miRNA, indicates that MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 miRNA form a regulatory loop with negative feedback.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mutual regulation data.

claim: YFP fluorescence, indicative of MpFRH1 promoter activity, was observed in the rhizoid precursor cells of proMpFRH1:3xYFP:NLS transformed plants.
source: We observed YFP fluorescence, indicative of MpFRH1 promoter activity, in the rhizoid precursor cells, which on young gemmae can be distinguished from non-rhizoid precursor cells based on their strongly reduced chlorophyll autofluorescence (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The YFP signal persisted in elongating rhizoids.
source: The YFP signal persisted in elongating rhizoids (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: MpIRE promoter expression was detected in both rhizoid precursor cells and non-rhizoid precursor cells.
source: MpIRE promoter expression was detected in both rhizoid precursor cells and non-rhizoid precursor cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strong proFRH1:3xYFP:NLS signal detected in rhizoid precursor cells results from stronger MpFRH1 promoter activity in these cells than in surrounding cells.
source: These results suggest that the strong proFRH1:3xYFP:NLS signal detected in rhizoid precursor cells results from stronger MpFRH1 promoter activity in these cells than in surrounding cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of MpFRH1 and MpIRE promoter expression patterns.

claim: Strong MpFRH1 promoter activity was observed in mucilage papillae that form near the gemmae meristematic region of 1 day old gemmae.
source: In addition, we observed strong MpFRH1 promoter activity in mucilage papillae that form near the gemmae meristematic region of 1 day old gemmae (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Some mucilage papillae were observed without YFP signal, suggesting that MpFRH1 is transiently expressed during mucilage papilla development.
source: We also observed some mucilage papillae without YFP signal, suggesting that MpFRH1 is transiently expressed during mucilage papilla development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of variable YFP signal in mucilage papillae.

claim: MpFRH1 is expressed in epidermal cells that develop rhizoids and papillae.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that MpFRH1 is expressed in epidermal cells that develop rhizoids and papillae.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the promoter-reporter expression data.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA binding site is 100% conserved in all twelve liverwort species for which RSL class I transcript sequence data was available through the 1000 plants project.
source: The FRH1 miRNA binding site is 100% conserved in all twelve liverwort species for which RSL class I transcript sequence data was available through the 1000 plants project (https://db.cngb.org/onekp/, Figure 8, a longer region of the alignment is provided in Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 8.

claim: There is no MpFRH1 binding site sequence in the class I RSL transcripts of the moss P. patens, the lycophyte S. Kraussiana or the angiosperm A. thaliana.
source: There is no MpFRH1 binding site sequence in the class I RSL transcripts of the moss P. patens, the lycophyte S. Kraussiana or the angiosperm A. thaliana.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: While the regulation of RSL class I genes by FRH1-like miRNAs became established early in the liverwort lineage, different negative regulation evolved in other lineages.
source: Together, these data suggest that while the regulation of RSL class I genes by FRH1-like miRNAs became established early in the liverwort lineage, different negative regulation evolved in other lineages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the conservation pattern of the FRH1 target site.

claim: The genomic sequence 3.5 kb upstream of MpRSL1 does not contain any L1-box sequences.
source: The genomic sequence 3.5 kb upstream of MpRSL1 does not contain any L1-box sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: The MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates MpRSL1 in M. polymorpha and there is no evidence for a role of class IV homeodomain protein in the negative regulation of MpRSL1 expression.
source: Therefore, the MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates MpRSL1 in M. polymorpha and we find no evidence for a role of class IV homeodomain protein in the negative regulation of MpRSL1 expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the absence of L1-box sequences and the experimental data on MpFRH1 function.

claim: The discovery that a miRNA represses RSL class I function in liverworts demonstrates that different mechanisms of negative regulation of these conserved transcription factors evolved in the liverworts and angiosperms.
source: The discovery that a miRNA represses RSL class I function in liverworts demonstrates that different mechanisms of negative regulation of these conserved transcription factors evolved in the liverworts and angiosperms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparative data on negative regulation mechanisms.

claim: AtGL2 is the only repressor of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 to have been identified to date.
source: To date, AtGL2 is the only repressor of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 to have been identified.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the current literature on Arabidopsis root hair regulation.

claim: There are no FRH1 miRNA target sequences in either AtRHD6 or AtRSL1 mRNA and the FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in A. thaliana or any other angiosperm.
source: There are no FRH1 miRNA target sequences in either AtRHD6 or AtRSL1 mRNA and the FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in A. thaliana or any other angiosperm.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and database searches.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA does not regulate AtRHD6 or AtRSL1 in A. thaliana.
source: This demonstrates that the FRH1 miRNA does not regulate these genes in A. thaliana.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the absence of FRH1 target sites in Arabidopsis RSL genes.

claim: At least two independent mechanisms that negatively regulate the ancient RSL class I gene mediated differentiation module have evolved among land plants.
source: The observation that RSL class I genes are repressed by a miRNA and a homeodomain-leucine-zipper transcription factor in M. polymorpha and A. thaliana respectively demonstrates that at least two independent mechanisms that negatively regulate the ancient RSL class I gene mediated differentiation module have evolved among land plants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparative data on negative regulation mechanisms.

claim: It is likely that different modes of negative regulation for RSL class I genes have evolved more than twice during the course of land plant evolution.
source: It is likely that different modes of negative regulation for RSL class I genes have evolved more than twice during the course of land plant evolution.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the limited data on negative regulation in other lineages.

claim: The RSL class I genes PpRSL1 and PpRSL2 promote rhizoid and mucilage papilla development in the moss P. patens, but nothing is known about their negative regulation.
source: The RSL class I genes PpRSL1 and PpRSL2 promote rhizoid and mucilage papilla development in the moss P. patens (Menand et al., 2007; Proust et al., 2016), but nothing is known about their negative regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and knowledge of the current state of the field.

claim: RSL class I genes also positively regulate root hair development in the grasses Oryza sativa and Brachypodium distachyon, but the mechanism of their negative regulation is unknown.
source: Similarly, RSL class I genes also positively regulate root hair development in the grasses Oryza sativa and Brachypodium distachyon (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017), but the mechanism of their negative regulation is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and knowledge of the current state of the field.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA target sites are not conserved in RSL class I mRNAs of moss or grasses and FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in either mosses or grasses.
source: The FRH1 miRNA target sites are not conserved in these RSL class I mRNAs and FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in either mosses or grasses.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and database searches.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA is unlikely to act as negative regulator outside the liverworts.
source: Therefore, the FRH1 miRNA is unlikely to act as negative regulator outside the liverworts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of conservation of FRH1 target sites outside liverworts.

claim: Other modes for the negative regulation of RSL class I genes evolved among other lineages, but they remain to be discovered.
source: We conclude that other modes for the negative regulation of RSL class I genes evolved among other lineages, but they remain to be discovered.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the comparative data.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA is only found in one monophyletic lineage of land plants, the liverworts.
source: MpFRH1 miRNA is only found in one monophyletic lineage of land plants, the liverworts.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA has been conserved since the divergence of the two major clades of liverworts – Marchantiopsida and Jungermanniopsida – estimated to have occurred more than 405 million years ago.
source: It has been conserved since the divergence of the two major clades of liverworts – Marchantiopsida and Jungermanniopsida – estimated to have occurred more than 405 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the conservation data and citation to prior phylogenetic research.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA may have existed since soon after the divergence of liverworts from other land plant lineages approximately 440 million years ago.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the FRH1 miRNA may have existed since soon after the divergence of liverworts from other land plant lineages approximately 440 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the conservation data and citation to prior phylogenetic research.

claim: Although the negative regulatory mechanisms have changed in different lineages, FRH1 mediated negative regulation of RSL class I genes has been extant since a period in Earth history when the radiation in morphological diversity of land plants occurred.
source: This indicates that although the negative regulatory mechanisms have changed in different lineages, FRH1 mediated negative regulation of RSL class I genes has been extant since a period in Earth history when the radiation in morphological diversity of land plants occurred.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the conservation and timing data.

claim: The appearance of the FRH1 miRNA may have been associated with gene regulatory network rewiring that occurred during the morphological diversification early in the liverwort lineage or during the evolution of liverworts from a common, non-liverwort ancestor.
source: The appearance of the FRH1 miRNA may have been associated with gene regulatory network rewiring that occurred during the morphological diversification early in the liverwort lineage or during the evolution of liverworts from a common, non-liverwort ancestor.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the evolutionary significance of FRH1 miRNA origin.

claim: Negative regulators can define when and where positive regulators are expressed and therefore are a key component in any gene regulatory network.
source: Negative regulators can define when and where positive regulators are expressed and therefore are a key component in any gene regulatory network.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about gene regulatory networks.

claim: Many mechanisms for spatial patterning of cell differentiation are based on lateral inhibition by mobile negative regulators.
source: For example, many mechanisms for spatial patterning of cell differentiation are based on lateral inhibition by mobile negative regulators.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about developmental patterning mechanisms.

claim: The delta-notch signalling system defines spacing patterns of different cell types in metazoan tissues and organs based on the principle of lateral inhibition.
source: This principle underpins the delta-notch signalling system that defines spacing patterns of different cell types in metazoan tissues and organs (Collier et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on delta-notch signaling.

claim: CAPRICE family of mobile negative transcriptional regulators control the pattern of root epidermal cell differentiation in A. thaliana.
source: Another example are the CAPRICE family of mobile negative transcriptional regulators that control the pattern of root epidermal cell differentiation in A. thaliana.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Arabidopsis root hair patterning.

claim: CAPRICE proteins are expressed in non-hair cells, but accumulate in hair-forming cells where they form a protein complex that binds to the promoter of AtGL2 repressing its transcription.
source: CAPRICE proteins are expressed in non-hair cells, but accumulate in hair-forming cells where they form a protein complex that binds to the promoter of AtGL2 repressing its transcription (Wada et al., 2002; Schellmann et al., 2002; Kurata et al., 2005; Lee and Schiefelbein, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on CAPRICE function.

claim: CAPRICE-mediated AtGL2 repression facilitates RSL class I expression, which then promotes the differentiation of root hair cells.
source: CAPRICE-mediated AtGL2 repression facilitates RSL class I expression, which then promotes the differentiation of root hair cells (Lin et al., 2015; Wada et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the CAPRICE-GL2-RSL regulatory pathway.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA produced in cells that go on to develop a rhizoid, mucilage papilla or gemma may negatively regulate RSL class I expression in surrounding cells and may have a role in the spatial specification of cell types during patterning the outer surface of the liverwort body.
source: MpFRH1 miRNA produced in cells that go on to develop a rhizoid, mucilage papilla or gemma may negatively regulate RSL class I expression in surrounding cells and may have a role in the spatial specification of cell types during patterning the outer surface of the liverwort body.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the potential role of MpFRH1 in spatial patterning.

claim: Repression of rhizoid, mucilage papilla or gemma differentiation could involve the non-cell autonomous repression of MpRSL1 expression by mobile MpFRH1 miRNA.
source: Therefore, repression of rhizoid, mucilage papilla or gemma differentiation could involve the non-cell autonomous repression of MpRSL1 expression by mobile MpFRH1 miRNA.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the potential mechanism of MpFRH1 action.

claim: The final cell size in elongating Arabidopsis root hairs is defined by RSL class II gene AtRSL4, which positively regulates root hair elongation, and two transcription factors AtGTL1 and AtDF1, which negatively regulate root hair elongation by directly repressing the transcription of AtRSL4 and other genes involved in root hair elongation.
source: For example, the final cell size in elongating Arabidopsis root hairs is defined by RSL class II gene AtRSL4, which positively regulates root hair elongation, and two transcription factors AtGTL1 and AtDF1, which negatively regulate root hair elongation by directly repressing the transcription of AtRSL4 and other genes involved in root hair elongation (Yi et al., 2010; Shibata et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on root hair elongation regulation.

claim: The Arabidopsis miRNA miR164 co-localises with its targets CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON1 (CUC1) and CUC2 transcription factor mRNAs in the margins of young leaf and floral primordia.
source: The Arabidopsis miRNA miR164 co-localises with its targets CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON1 (CUC1) and CUC2 transcription factor mRNAs in the margins of young leaf and floral primordia (Nikovics et al., 2006; Sieber et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on miR164 function.

claim: miR164 resistant CUC1 and CUC2 maintain the same expression domain as the wild type proteins, but are expressed at a higher level.
source: miR164 resistant CUC1 and CUC2 maintain the same expression domain as the wild type proteins, but are expressed at a higher level (Sieber et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on miR164-resistant CUC genes.

claim: miR164 functions to fine-tune the levels of CUC1 and CUC2 expression within their expression domain.
source: These findings suggest that miR164 functions to fine-tune the levels of CUC1 and CUC2 expression within their expression domain (Sieber et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited research on miR164 function.

claim: MpFRH1 may function in similar manner to miR164 by temporally fine-tuning MpRSL1 levels.
source: MpFRH1 may function in similar manner by temporally fine-tuning MpRSL1 levels.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the potential function of MpFRH1.

claim: It is possible that evolution of novel negative regulatory mechanisms was involved in the radiation of morphological diversity that followed the colonisation of the land by plants.
source: It is possible that evolution of novel negative regulatory mechanisms was involved in the radiation of morphological diversity that followed the colonisation of the land by plants.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the evolutionary significance of negative regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The morphology of extant streptophyte algae suggests that the streptophyte algal ancestors of land plants had little cell-type diversity and did not develop distinct organs.
source: The morphology of extant streptophyte algae suggests that the streptophyte algal ancestors of land plants had little cell-type diversity and did not develop distinct organs (McCourt et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on streptophyte algae morphology.

claim: Many transcription factor families previously thought to have evolved within land plants were already established in streptophyte algae.
source: However, recent studies demonstrate that many transcription factor families previously thought to have evolved within land plants were already established in streptophyte algae (Wilhelmsson et al., 2017; Hori et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on transcription factor evolution.

claim: The evolution of morphologically complex land plants from algal ancestors is likely to have involved the emergence of novel negative regulatory mechanisms around a core set of ancient transcription factors resulting in the evolution of novel gene regulatory networks that programmed novel morphologies.
source: The evolution of morphologically complex land plants from these algal ancestors is likely to have involved the emergence of novel negative regulatory mechanisms – such as miRNAs and transcriptional repressor proteins – around this core set of ancient transcription factors resulting in the evolution of novel gene regulatory networks that programmed novel morphologies.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the evolutionary mechanisms underlying land plant morphological evolution.

claim: The evolution of new and distinct negative regulatory mechanisms in the different lineages may have underpinned the radiation of morphological diversity in the stem groups of the major lineages of land plants.
source: Furthermore, the evolution of new and distinct negative regulatory mechanisms in the different lineages may have underpinned the radiation of morphological diversity in the stem groups of the major lineages of land plants.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the evolutionary significance of lineage-specific negative regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The radiation in morphological diversity between the Ordovician and Late Devonian resulted, at least in part, from the evolution of novel negative regulatory activities that modulated more ancient and conserved gene regulatory networks.
source: If correct, it suggests that the radiation in morphological diversity between the Ordovician and Late Devonian resulted, at least in part, from the evolution of novel negative regulatory activities that modulated more ancient and conserved gene regulatory networks that are conserved in many extant land plant lineages.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the evolutionary mechanisms underlying early land plant diversification.

claim: This hypothesis can be tested by defining the mechanism of negative regulation of conserved gene regulatory networks that exist among the main lineages of land plants.
source: This hypothesis can be tested by defining the mechanism of negative regulation of conserved gene regulatory networks that exist among the main lineages of land plants.
evidence: This claim proposes a testable hypothesis for future research.
